chapter: Al Hibbler, Dakota Staton and later years
title: Testifying, the girls' letter, and an unknown verdict
summary: The defense lawyer cuts off his answers, he leaves before the jury returns, and he suspects the local boy walked away free.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Anyway, I got this letter from the Navy that these two girls were asking me if I would write to them and state to them what had happened in this case, and these two little girls, it seemed as if their backs had been broken or something. Of course, their parents were dead, and the third party in the car happened to be an uncle who was German, and they had been to New York to pick him up and bring him... This was his first time in the United States.
Anyway, this trial... I was up there two or three times - three times, I believe. The last time I was there, they had

me on the witness stand, and the defense lawyer asked me what condition was the highway in. Well, the Pennsylvania Turnpike I remember is about 300-some miles long. So I made mention of the fact, I said, "The turnpike is 300 miles long. What do you mean?" He said, "Well, any part of it." He said, "Well, I did see some people doing repair work." And he said "Oh, thank you." And I said, "But..." He said, "That's enough" -- and I stepped down. Another time he asked me some other question as to did I see men working on the highway or did I see anything wrong with the highway. When I would go to explain that this was not happening where the accident happened, I was never allowed to answer that. I would be told by the judge, "You can step down" or he would say, "Well, that's enough."

Well, when I left there, the jury was debating, and the last time I was there... I was playing a gig in Cleveland. It was one of those times when I had gone back to play a job with Al. And I had just gone up to this little town for the trial, and I had to get right back to Cleveland. So the jury was out, and the district attorney told me "Well, we won't need you any more." I said, "Well, okay. But do me a favor and send me a letter or something and let me know how the trial comes out." He said, "Oh, sure I will." I haven't heard from him since. And the last time I saw, the trial was going this

kid's way who had caused the accident. He was a Pennsylvania boy, you know. Well, I just surmised that those people are dead, those grown-ups and the kids, nothing you could do about them, and they just... These people lived somewhere out in the Midwest. So I imagine this boy, with the proper amount of money, just walked away clean from the whole thing.
